dish:Rosé de Provence (Côtes de Provence.name: Rosé de Provence (Côtes de Provence & Bandol)
dish:Rosé de Provence (Côtes de Provence.text: The true drink of this coast and the honest local product. Côtes de Provence is the region's giant AOC, and rosé is roughly 80 percent of what Provence makes — the pale, near-salmon style from short skin contact and cold fermentation. Just west, tiny Bandol (about 1,600 ha) makes a darker, structured, age-worthy rosé and red built on Mourvèdre. Drink it cold, young, and cheaper than the sea view suggests. Origin Var / Provence; Côtes de Provence and Bandol (Bandol AOC created 1941), vines here since Roman times

dish:Soupe de poissons de roche & rouill.name: Soupe de poissons de roche & rouille
dish:Soupe de poissons de roche & rouill.text: The everyday, unglamorous ancestor of bouillabaisse and the one you actually order here: rock fish too small to sell, simmered with tomato, saffron, olive oil and fennel, then sieved to a rust-coloured broth. Served with croutons, grated cheese and rouille — a garlic-and-saffron chilli mayonnaise you float on the bread. A fisherman's thrift dish, not a luxury. Origin Provençal coast, fishermen's cuisine; shares the Phocaean 'kakavia' root of Marseille

dish:Bouillabaisse.name: Bouillabaisse
dish:Bouillabaisse.text: The famous one, and worth being honest about: it is a Marseille dish, not a Cavalaire native, descended from the Phocaean fishermen's cauldron ('kakavia'). Several bony Mediterranean fish added one at a time to a saffron-and-fennel broth, the soup served first with rouille, the fish on a platter after. A real one is expensive and slow; a cheap 'bouillabaisse' on a tourist terrace is usually just fish soup — the 1980 Marseille Charter exists precisely because of that drift. Origin Marseille (Greek Phocaean roots, ~600 BCE); Charter de la Bouillabaisse, 1980

dish:Aïoli (le grand aïoli).name: Aïoli (le grand aïoli)
dish:Aïoli (le grand aïoli).text: Less a sauce than a Friday institution: a stiff emulsion of garlic pounded with olive oil, served as the centrepiece of a spread of poached cod, boiled potatoes, carrots, green beans, snails and egg. Ancient Mediterranean in root, mentioned in medieval Provençal texts. Order it on a day you have nowhere to be. Origin Provence / wider Mediterranean; garlic-and-oil emulsion of great antiquity

dish:Tapenade.name: Tapenade
dish:Tapenade.text: The apéritif of the coast: black (or green) olives, capers, anchovy, garlic and olive oil pounded to a dark paste, spread on bread with that first glass of rosé. The name comes from Provençal 'tapena', caper. Its invention is traditionally credited to a Marseille chef around 1880 — plausible, and worth hedging. Origin Marseille, credited to around 1880 (attribution traditional, not certain)

dish:Panisses.name: Panisses
dish:Panisses.text: Chickpea-flour cooked to a paste, set, sliced and fried into golden batons — crisp outside, soft within, eaten with salt like chips. A working-class street food that came to Marseille's Estaque district with Ligurian and Piedmontese immigrants in the 19th century. Cousin of Nice's socca, but cut thick and fried. Origin Marseille (Estaque), 19th century; Ligurian/Piedmontese roots

dish:Daube provençale.name: Daube provençale
dish:Daube provençale.text: The winter dish of the Var interior: beef cut in big chunks, marinated overnight in Provençal red wine, then simmered for hours with pork belly, carrots, tomato, black olives, orange peel and a bouquet of thyme and bay. Born as a preservation and thrift dish, now the region's Sunday and celebration stew — the leftovers traditionally sauce a plate of ravioli. Origin Provence; a medieval/early-modern braise, elevated over time

dish:Pieds et paquets.name: Pieds et paquets
dish:Pieds et paquets.text: For the curious: lamb tripe rolled into little parcels around pork belly, garlic and parsley (the 'paquets'), stewed slowly with lamb trotters (the 'pieds') in white wine and tomato. A 19th-century Marseille workers' dish, still an emblem of Provençal winter tables — offal-forward and not for everyone, which is exactly why it's genuine. Origin Marseille, 19th century (Sisteron also claims a version)

dish:Tarte tropézienne.name: Tarte tropézienne
dish:Tarte tropézienne.text: The one truly local sweet, from over the capes: a sugar-crusted brioche split and filled with a blend of pastry cream and buttercream. Created in Saint-Tropez in 1955 by Polish-born baker Alexandre Micka; Brigitte Bardot, filming 'And God Created Woman', is said to have suggested the name, which Micka trademarked in 1973. The closest thing to a hometown dessert on this gulf. Origin Saint-Tropez, 1955, Alexandre Micka; named c.1956, trademarked 1973

coffee-scene:RAWr Torréfaction.label: Cogolin (Galerie Raimu
coffee-scene:RAWr Torréfaction.hook: The nearest thing to a real third-wave cup on the gulf: a small workshop that green-roasts its own beans on site, pours them across a brew bar, and sells kit and organic/matcha teas alongside. Order whatever single origin came off the drum that week and take a bag home.

coffee-scene:Le Jardin du Café.label: Hyères (9 rue Massillon
coffee-scene:Le Jardin du Café.hook: Worth the drive if you take coffee seriously. Sylvain Daronian roasts around fifteen origins daily behind the counter of a tiny épicerie-torréfaction; you come to talk grind and method as much as to buy. Doubles as a fine grocery of Provençal oils and honeys.

coffee-scene:Soeurs Coffee & Bakery.name: Soeurs Coffee & Bakery
coffee-scene:Soeurs Coffee & Bakery.label: Cavalaire-sur-Mer (in town)
coffee-scene:Soeurs Coffee & Bakery.hook: The honest truth: Cavalaire itself has no serious roaster, and Soeurs is the best in-town option — a coffee-shop-bakery-brunch run by Matthieu and Valentin, good for a flat white with a viennoiserie rather than a hunt for terroir beans. Treat it as convenience, not pilgrimage.

natural-wine:La Grange à Vins.label: La Croix-Valmer (248 rue du 8 mai 1945) — ~12 min from Cavalaire
natural-wine:La Grange à Vins.hook: The one to book. A caviste-comptoir where the pours run classic to natural, the boards are homemade charcuterie and cheese, and musicians turn up in the evenings. Ask the counter to steer you toward the living bottles rather than the safe rosé.

natural-wine:Fondugues-Pradugues.label: Ramatuelle (in the vines

natural-wine:Le Clos des B.label: Grimaud — ~30 min
natural-wine:Le Clos des B.hook: A tiny natural grower to look for on gulf wine lists (including at HERA and La Grange): cuvées made without additives and fermented on their own indigenous yeasts. Not a slick tasting room — a small, personal project, but it does run introduction-to-natural-wine tastings on site.

listening:Festival Face à la Mer.label: Cavalaire-sur-Mer (Esplanade Sainte-Estelle

listening:Jazz à Ramatuelle.label: Ramatuelle
listening:Jazz à Ramatuelle.hook: Late-June nights of international jazz in a stone open-air amphitheatre, the music threading through cicadas and garrigue — one of Provence's oldest and least corporate jazz gatherings. Honest caveat: no 2026 edition was programmed, so treat it as a future-year plan, not a fixture, and check before you count on it.

listening:Musée de l'Annonciade.label: Saint-Tropez (former chapel

around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.label: ~15 min east along the Corniche des Maures
around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.hook: A 20-hectare estate tumbling to a private cove, planted as a living atlas of the world's Mediterranean-climate floras — Chile, California, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries.
around:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.text: A 20-hectare estate tumbling to a private cove, planted as a living atlas of the world's Mediterranean-climate floras — Chile, California, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries. The garden was designed by landscaper Gilles Clément and the estate is owned by the Conservatoire du littoral, which acquired it in 1989; from June to September you can snorkel its guided 'Sentier Marin' straight off the garden's own beach.

around:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coastal.name: Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coastal path
around:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coastal.label: ~15–25 min (trailheads at Gigaro or l'Escalet)
around:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coastal.hook: The wild, undeveloped tip of the Saint-Tropez peninsula: a marked sentier du littoral through pines and garrigue to a slim sandy isthmus joining Cap Taillat to the mainland.
around:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coastal.text: The wild, undeveloped tip of the Saint-Tropez peninsula: a marked sentier du littoral through pines and garrigue to a slim sandy isthmus joining Cap Taillat to the mainland. Protected by the Conservatoire du littoral, so no villas — rare here; from the ridge a 360° view takes in the Maures, Cap Camarat lighthouse and the Îles d'Hyères. A dolmen (Briande) hides in the interior.

around:Gassin.name: Gassin
around:Gassin.label: ~25 min
around:Gassin.hook: A medieval village stacked at 200 m with bougainvillea-hung facades and the Androuno, at ~29 cm reputed to be one of the narrowest streets in the world.
around:Gassin.text: A medieval village stacked at 200 m with bougainvillea-hung facades and the Androuno, at ~29 cm reputed to be one of the narrowest streets in the world. Classed among Les Plus Beaux Villages de France; its ridge gives a full 360° sweep over the gulf, the Îles d'Or and, on clear days, the Alps — the peninsula's best free panorama.

around:Ramatuelle.name: Ramatuelle
around:Ramatuelle.label: ~25–30 min
around:Ramatuelle.hook: A concentric hilltop village of vaulted passages and honey stone, ringed by the vineyards that climb toward Pampelonne.
around:Ramatuelle.text: A concentric hilltop village of vaulted passages and honey stone, ringed by the vineyards that climb toward Pampelonne. Its Théâtre de Verdure hosts the jazz and theatre festivals; below it lie the biodynamic estates (Fondugues-Pradugues) and the AOC Côtes de Provence vines of the peninsula.

around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.name: Bormes-les-Mimosas
around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.label: ~35 min west
around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.hook: A cascading flowered old town above the sea, famous for its mimosa, which erupts yellow from January to March across some 90 species.
around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.text: A cascading flowered old town above the sea, famous for its mimosa, which erupts yellow from January to March across some 90 species. Newly classed among Les Plus Beaux Villages de France (label awarded September 2024); a microclimate lets hundreds of plant species grow through its cobbled lanes — effectively an open-air garden village.

around:Collobrières & the Chartreuse de.name: Collobrières & the Chartreuse de la Verne
around:Collobrières & the Chartreuse de.label: ~40 min inland, into the Massif des Maures
around:Collobrières & the Chartreuse de.hook: The chestnut capital of the Maures (come for marrons glacés and chestnut cream), paired with a lonely 12th-century Carthusian monastery deep in the cork-oak forest.
around:Collobrières & the Chartreuse de.text: The chestnut capital of the Maures (come for marrons glacés and chestnut cream), paired with a lonely 12th-century Carthusian monastery deep in the cork-oak forest. The Chartreuse de la Verne (founded 1170), restored in the Maures' green serpentine stone, has since 1983 sheltered a silent community of the sisters of Bethlehem — the best-preserved charterhouse in Provence, reached by a forest road.

around:Îles d'Hyères — Porquerolles & Po.name: Îles d'Hyères — Porquerolles & Port-Cros
around:Îles d'Hyères — Porquerolles & Po.label: Day trip; seasonal ferry from Cavalaire/La Croix-Valmer (~May–Sept), year-round from Le Lavandou
around:Îles d'Hyères — Porquerolles & Po.hook: The 'Golden Islands': Porquerolles with white-sand beaches, vineyards and the Fondation Carmignac art villa; Port-Cros a car-free forested peak ringed by clear water.
around:Îles d'Hyères — Porquerolles & Po.text: The 'Golden Islands': Porquerolles with white-sand beaches, vineyards and the Fondation Carmignac art villa; Port-Cros a car-free forested peak ringed by clear water. Port-Cros became Europe's oldest marine national park in 1963; both are protected, so the crowds thin the moment you leave the village quay. Boats run with Vedettes Îles d'Or & Le Corsaire.

around:Corniche des Maures pocket coves.name: Corniche des Maures pocket coves
around:Corniche des Maures pocket coves.label: The coast road itself, 5–25 min between Cavalaire and Le Lavandou
around:Corniche des Maures pocket coves.hook: The scenic corniche linking Cavalaire to Le Lavandou, strung with small pine-backed beaches — Le Rayol, Le Canadel, Cavalière, Pramousquier.
around:Corniche des Maures pocket coves.text: The scenic corniche linking Cavalaire to Le Lavandou, strung with small pine-backed beaches — Le Rayol, Le Canadel, Cavalière, Pramousquier. Quieter, greener and less built-up than Pampelonne's club-beaches; the Massif des Maures drops almost straight into the sea here, so the coves stay wild and pine-shaded.

drink:Côtes de Provence Rosé — the pale,.name: Côtes de Provence Rosé — the pale, bone-dry archetype
drink:Côtes de Provence Rosé — the pale,.hook: The colour is a decision, not a dilution: these rosés are direct-pressed or briefly macerated, so the pink stays onion-skin pale while the wine drinks bone-dry and saline — the vines sit close enough to the sea to taste it. It is not the sweet blush the tint suggests. One thing to carry: buy the youngest vintage on the shelf and drink it cold this summer, not next.

drink:Cru Classé Rosé — Provence's own 1.name: Cru Classé Rosé — Provence's own 1955 ranking
drink:Cru Classé Rosé — Provence's own 1.hook: Long before today's appellation rules, a 1955 ministerial decree classified a handful of Provence estates; of the original list, eighteen still carry the words 'Cru Classé' on the label, and Domaine de la Croix — founded 1882, left derelict, then bought and wholly replanted after 2001 — is one of them. On the schist and clay above the bay it makes a rosé with more grip and density than the crowd. The pedigree is real, but it was awarded on seniority, not a tasting — a fact worth knowing before you pay for it.

drink:Seaside sand-terroir Rosé with Tib.name: Seaside sand-terroir Rosé with Tibouren
drink:Seaside sand-terroir Rosé with Tib.hook: Tibouren is the peninsula's old grape — savoury, faintly orange-tinged, scented with garrigue rather than fruit-candy, and long tied to this stretch of the Saint-Tropez coast. On the sandy, wind-scoured strips between Cap Lardier and Cap Taillat, where Bastide Blanche's vines run nearly to the cliff, it gives a rosé that smells of hot pine and salt. Both houses are certified organic; taste this against a supermarket Provence and you learn what 'saline' actually means. (Bastide Blanche and La Croix are one estate under two labels — don't chase them as rivals.)

drink:Côtes de Provence Blanc — Rolle by.name: Côtes de Provence Blanc — Rolle by the water
drink:Côtes de Provence Blanc — Rolle by.hook: Rolle is simply the local name for Vermentino, and by this coast it turns out a white of citrus pith and sea-spray minerality — the natural partner to the fishermen's morning catch on the quay. It is far rarer than the rosé and rarely leaves the region; if you see it, that is the bottle to carry back to the boat.

drink:Pastis — the shore aperitif ritual.name: Pastis — the shore aperitif ritual
drink:Pastis — the shore aperitif ritual.hook: The ritual is fixed: a measure of pastis, then roughly five of cold water poured over ice until the clear spirit clouds — the 'louche' — drunk before lunch in the shade. Henri Bardouin blends more than 65 plants and spices where the industrial anise leans on a handful. Honest caveat: it is distilled inland at Forcalquier, in the Haute-Provence back-country, not on the coast — the seaside owns the ritual, the hills own the bottle.

landmarks:Espace Archéologique Municipal.name: Espace Archéologique Municipal Aristide Fabre
landmarks:Espace Archéologique Municipal.hook: The town's small municipal archaeological room — on the ground floor of the médiathèque — tracing Cavalaire's deep past through collections, models and panels: the Iron Age oppidum of Montjean, and above all the Gallo-Roman villas of Pardigon, which made and shipped wine from this very coast. It is the honest key to the 'Heraclea Caccabaria' story — the port that Roman sailing itineraries record here — because nothing of the ancient harbour still stands above water; what survives of it is gathered, in fragments, in this one room. Rotating exhibitions supplement the permanent display.

landmarks:Port de Cavalaire — the ancien.name: Port de Cavalaire — the ancient Heraclea anchorage
landmarks:Port de Cavalaire — the ancien.hook: This deep, south-facing bay is generally identified as the old port of Heraclea Caccabaria, named in the Roman Antonine Itinerary — a well-sheltered anchorage screened from the Mistral, which is exactly why Greek, then Roman, then medieval traders used it. Small fishing boats (the traditional pointus) still work it, and the crews sell the morning catch on the quay. No ancient masonry survives above water; the harbour's real relic is the shelter itself.

landmarks:Église Saint-Laurent.name: Église Saint-Laurent
landmarks:Église Saint-Laurent.hook: The parish church — and a lesson in how young the resort town is. Begun in 1910 as a modest chapel dependent on the older hill-village of Gassin, enlarged in 1932, it became a parish in its own right only in 1960. Not a medieval monument: it is the stone record of Cavalaire's early-20th-century birth as a seaside town.

landmarks:Monument du Débarquement de Pr.name: Monument du Débarquement de Provence
landmarks:Monument du Débarquement de Pr.hook: A granite twin-column memorial (by architect G. Nadal, 2nd Grand Prix de Rome) to the Allied landing of 15–16 August 1944, Operation Dragoon. Cavalaire's beach was codenamed 'Alpha'; General de Lattre's Army B came ashore here on 16 August. This — not a medieval castle — is the town's true fortification story: the German coastal defences of the so-called 'Mur de la Méditerranée' were overrun in the days that followed. Three granite blocks nearby mark the 1st DFL and US units.

landmarks:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin d.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
landmarks:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin d.hook: A 20-hectare protected domain of the Conservatoire du littoral, its gardens designed by landscape architect Gilles Clément to gather the world's Mediterranean-climate floras — California, Chile, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries — around an early-20th-century villa above a private cove. In summer a guided 'sentier marin' lets you snorkel the protected Baie du Figuier. The finest single outing near Cavalaire, and a real botanical education, not a municipal flowerbed.

landmarks:Cap Lardier.name: Cap Lardier
landmarks:Cap Lardier.hook: The wild southern headland of the Saint-Tropez peninsula, its ~300-hectare pine massif bought by the Conservatoire du littoral in 1978 to save it from development — a coast path from Gigaro beach threads pines, cistus and rock-rose to empty sand coves, with the Bastide Blanche and La Croix vines running almost to the cliff edge. It ties the wine, the walk and the 1944 'Alpha' beaches into one afternoon. A natural site, not a building: there is no road to the point.

culture:Monument du Débarquement, Plage.name: Monument du Débarquement, Plage de Cavalaire (Alpha Beach)
culture:Monument du Débarquement, Plage.hook: An open-air landing memorial on the seafront promenade, marking where the Allied invasion of southern France came ashore. Free, always open; walk it, don't queue for it.
culture:Monument du Débarquement, Plage.text: An open-air landing memorial on the seafront promenade, marking where the Allied invasion of southern France came ashore. Free, always open; walk it, don't queue for it. The terroir truth locals live with: this mild holiday bay was code-named Alpha Beach. On 15 August 1944, Operation Dragoon — the 'other' D-Day that history forgets behind Normandy — put the US 3rd Infantry Division ashore right here. The following evening, around 7pm on 16 August, General Jean de Lattre's Army B (the French First Army, eventually a quarter-million men drawn from the Free French and the Army of Africa) began landing at Cavalaire and drove north up the Rhône to help free France. The sand you're sunbathing on is a place of remembrance. One real thing: France was liberated from the south as well as the north. Signal Verified: Operation Dragoon landings 15 Aug 1944 (Alpha Beach = Cavalaire, US 3rd Infantry Division); de Lattre's Army B began landing ~7pm on 16 Aug 1944; monument on the Promenade de la Mer — Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourism

culture:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
culture:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.hook: A ~20-hectare hillside garden (about 7 ha planted) that sets the world's Mediterranean-climate regions side by side — Chile, California, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries — tumbling down to the Baie du Figuier opposite the Golden Isles.
culture:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des.text: A ~20-hectare hillside garden (about 7 ha planted) that sets the world's Mediterranean-climate regions side by side — Chile, California, South Africa, Australia, the Canaries — tumbling down to the Baie du Figuier opposite the Golden Isles. Terroir made literal: the Var coast rebuilt as a living atlas of every dry-summer climate on earth. Begun in 1910 as the retreat of Parisian businessman Alfred Courmes (his first villa became the Hôtel de la Mer), bought in 1940 by aviation magnate Henry Potez who added an Art-Deco garden, then left to run wild for years. In 1989 the Conservatoire du Littoral rescued it and handed the redesign to Gilles Clément, the gardener-philosopher of the 'jardin en mouvement.' You learn the idea of climatic analogues — why a Cape Town protea and a Californian ceanothus thrive in the same Provençal soil. Signal Verified: created 1910 (Courmes, a Parisian businessman; his first house became the Hôtel de la Mer), Potez from 1940, saved 1989 by Conservatoire du Littoral, redesigned by Gilles Clément; ~20 ha, more than 4,000 species today — Wikipedia / Conservatoire du littoral

culture:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol (under.name: Le Sentier Marin du Rayol (underwater snorkel trail)
culture:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol (under.hook: A guided snorkel — wetsuit, mask, fins — over the protected seagrass meadows of the Baie du Figuier, led by a state-certified guide. About 2 hours, 45 minutes in the water, from €37 (garden entry included). Summer only, book ahead, age 8+ and must be able to swim.
culture:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol (under.text: A guided snorkel — wetsuit, mask, fins — over the protected seagrass meadows of the Baie du Figuier, led by a state-certified guide. About 2 hours, 45 minutes in the water, from €37 (garden entry included). Summer only, book ahead, age 8+ and must be able to swim. The garden's story continued below the waterline. The same Conservatoire-protected bay hides prairies of Posidonia, urchins, damselfish and, if you're lucky, an octopus — the identical seabed as the Îles d'Hyères offshore. The one real thing you'll carry away: Posidonia is not seaweed but a flowering plant that beds down underwater, one of the Mediterranean's great oxygen engines and a nursery for everything else. A quiet, low-ego alternative to the peninsula's show-off beaches. Signal Verified: guided sentier marin, ~2 hrs / 45 min in water, adult €37 (garden entry included), from age 8 — Domaine du Rayol official site / Golfe de Saint-Tropez Tourisme

culture:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coasta.name: Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coastal path
culture:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coasta.hook: The sentier du littoral rounding two of the peninsula's three wild capes — a coastal out along the bays of Cavalaire and Briande to the sand isthmus of Cap Taillat, with an inland wooded return. The full loop is ~14 km / 4 hours; you can turn back early at Cap Lardier.
culture:Cap Lardier & Cap Taillat coasta.text: The sentier du littoral rounding two of the peninsula's three wild capes — a coastal out along the bays of Cavalaire and Briande to the sand isthmus of Cap Taillat, with an inland wooded return. The full loop is ~14 km / 4 hours; you can turn back early at Cap Lardier. These are the last undeveloped headlands on the whole Saint-Tropez peninsula — and the reason is the point of the walk. The Conservatoire du Littoral bought and protects the three sibling capes (Camarat, Taillat, Lardier), which is why there are pines and cistus here instead of villas. From the high point of Cap Lardier a 180° sweep takes in the Camarat lighthouse, Cap Taillat's tombolo of sand, the Îles du Levant and back across the Cavalaire bay. One real thing: on this coast, 'wild' means publicly bought, not accidentally spared. Signal Verified: capes protected by the Conservatoire du Littoral, loop ~14 km / ~4 hrs from Gigaro, 180° summit panorama (Camarat lighthouse, Cap Taillat, Îles du Levant) — AllTrails / Visorando / Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourism

culture:Sentier du Fenouillet, Corniche.name: Sentier du Fenouillet, Corniche des Maures
culture:Sentier du Fenouillet, Corniche.hook: Cavalaire's own home walk: a signposted coastal stretch from Plage de Bonporteau toward Pointe du Dattier, looping back through a shaded valley. Shorten to ~3 km or push the full ~8 km — moderate, with a few steep sections, not a scramble.
culture:Sentier du Fenouillet, Corniche.text: Cavalaire's own home walk: a signposted coastal stretch from Plage de Bonporteau toward Pointe du Dattier, looping back through a shaded valley. Shorten to ~3 km or push the full ~8 km — moderate, with a few steep sections, not a scramble. No car needed — this is the maquis on the town's doorstep. The path threads fragrant scrubland (cistus, pine, strawberry-tree) and coastal cliff, opening onto high views over the Îles d'Hyères and across to Cap Lardier; the damp valley on the return is a surprise in this sun-baked corner. The name to learn: the Massif des Maures, whose dark schist and cork-oak give the range its brooding look — a different, older geology from the pale limestone of the eastern Riviera (the name is usually traced to a Provençal word for 'dark,' though a link to the Moors is also cited). Signal Verified: Sentier du Fenouillet / Corniche des Maures from Plage de Bonporteau to Le Dattier, ~3 km short / ~8 km full (3 hrs, ~360 m gain) — Ville de Cavalaire / Côte d'Azur France / Provence-Guide

culture:Gassin.name: Gassin
culture:Gassin.hook: A medieval hill-village ringed by a rampart-walk terrace — the Promenade/Place deï Barri — shaded by centuries-old hackberry trees, with restaurant balconies hanging over the whole gulf. Best at dusk, when the day-trippers thin.
culture:Gassin.text: A medieval hill-village ringed by a rampart-walk terrace — the Promenade/Place deï Barri — shaded by centuries-old hackberry trees, with restaurant balconies hanging over the whole gulf. Best at dusk, when the day-trippers thin. Officially one of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, Gassin sits some 200 m up with a commanding read of the coast — its founders built high precisely to see sea-raiders coming, and that defensive height is now the finest free viewpoint around: in one slow turn you take in the Bay of Saint-Tropez, the dark Massif des Maures and the Golden Isles. The oddity to hunt for: l'Androuno, a lane just 29 cm wide, claimed among the narrowest streets in the world. Signal Verified: classed Plus Beaux Villages de France, ~200 m elevation, Place/Promenade deï Barri panorama over the bay of Cavalaire and the Îles d'Or, l'Androuno ~29 cm wide — Saint-Tropez Tourisme / Wikipedia (L'Androuno)

hotel-bars:Bar 1904, Château de la Messa.name: Bar 1904, Château de la Messardière (Airelles)
hotel-bars:Bar 1904, Château de la Messa.hook: A dappled-terrace lounge by day, low-lit speakeasy by night, inside a turreted château hotel looking over the Bay of Saint-Tropez and its own park. Come for one impeccable drink, not the room rate.
hotel-bars:Bar 1904, Château de la Messa.text: A dappled-terrace lounge by day, low-lit speakeasy by night, inside a turreted château hotel looking over the Bay of Saint-Tropez and its own park. Come for one impeccable drink, not the room rate. This is, plausibly, one of the very first bars the Côte d'Azur ever had. The château was a 19th-century wedding gift from cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac to his daughter Louise. In 1904 Madame de La Messardière began serving refreshments to her glamorous Belle Époque guests — opening what the house counts among the Riviera's earliest bars, and the year the bar takes its name from. It became Airelles' palace after a top-to-bottom restoration, reopening in July 2021. The terroir note: Saint-Tropez's aperitif culture is older and grander than the yacht-set cliché suggests. Honesty: palace prices — a sundowner, not a night out. Signal Verified: refreshments first served 1904 (Mme de La Messardière), among the Côte d'Azur's first bars; Airelles grand reopening 1 July 2021 — Airelles official site

hotel-bars:Le Vista, Lily of the Valley.name: Le Vista, Lily of the Valley
hotel-bars:Le Vista, Lily of the Valley.hook: A west-facing bar and restaurant terrace on the hilltop above Gigaro, positioned to hand you a glass exactly as the sun drops behind the Îles d'Hyères.
hotel-bars:Le Vista, Lily of the Valley.text: A west-facing bar and restaurant terrace on the hilltop above Gigaro, positioned to hand you a glass exactly as the sun drops behind the Îles d'Hyères. Philippe Starck designed the whole resort — opened end of June 2019 — like a Californian villa crossed with the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, and then aimed its main terrace at the sunset. The terroir logic is simple and worth knowing: this is the peninsula's west-facing shoulder, so unlike Saint-Tropez proper the light sets over the sea and the Golden Isles here. Honesty by negation: it's a design hotel, not weathered old Provence — dress, crowd and bill are all polished. Worth it for the golden hour. Signal Verified: opened late June 2019, architecture and interiors by Philippe Starck; Le Vista bar positioned to take in the sunset — Starck.com / Robb Report / Leading Hotels of the World

hotel-bars:La Brigantine — Lily of the V.name: La Brigantine — Lily of the Valley beach club, Gigaro
hotel-bars:La Brigantine — Lily of the V.hook: A feet-in-the-sand beach club and Italian kitchen at the quiet end of Gigaro, good for a late-afternoon glass with the sea a few metres away. A drink at the bar is the low-commitment way in; the sunbeds are beach-club priced.
hotel-bars:La Brigantine — Lily of the V.text: A feet-in-the-sand beach club and Italian kitchen at the quiet end of Gigaro, good for a late-afternoon glass with the sea a few metres away. A drink at the bar is the low-commitment way in; the sunbeds are beach-club priced. This is the golfe's sundowner ritual done on the peninsula's calm, west-facing side — the anti-Pampelonne. Here's the honest map, which matters more than any single address: Cavalaire's own long beach is a genuine public promenade (pedalos, gelato, families), lovely but not a polished-club scene; the terrace-drink culture sits a few minutes west at Gigaro; and the see-and-be-seen legends (Club 55, Loulou) are a further 30–40 minutes north at Pampelonne in Ramatuelle. Pick your shore by the mood you want. Signal Verified open 2026: Lily of the Valley's Brigantine beach club at the far end of Plage de Gigaro (beachfront Italian, chef Vincent Maillard), 2026 season Feb–Nov — Lily of the Valley official site / Excellence Riviera

walks:Le Sentier du Littoral — Les Trois.name: Le Sentier du Littoral — Les Trois Caps (Gigaro → Cap Lardier → Cap Taillat)
walks:Le Sentier du Littoral — Les Trois.hook: The signature coastal walk of this coast: from Gigaro beach the yellow-marked sentier hugs the sea to Cap Lardier, drops along the Briande bay to the sand isthmus of Cap Taillat, and loops back inland through cork oak and maquis. The full Gigaro loop is roughly 14 km / about 4 hours; you can also just walk out-and-back to a beach.
walks:Le Sentier du Littoral — Les Trois.text: The signature coastal walk of this coast: from Gigaro beach the yellow-marked sentier hugs the sea to Cap Lardier, drops along the Briande bay to the sand isthmus of Cap Taillat, and loops back inland through cork oak and maquis. The full Gigaro loop is roughly 14 km / about 4 hours; you can also just walk out-and-back to a beach. This is the last long undeveloped stretch of coast between Cavalaire and Saint-Tropez, and the reason is public money, not luck. Cap Lardier was classified under the 1930 landscape law (a site classé) back in 1966, then bought parcel by parcel by the Conservatoire du littoral from 1978 onward — it holds the longest protected coastal fringe of the three caps, some 6 km. It is managed with the Port-Cros National Park and the commune and has been a Natura 2000 zone since 2006. The lesson the walk teaches: villas stop exactly where the Conservatoire's boundary begins. Signal Cap Lardier classified under the 1930 law in 1966; acquired by the Conservatoire du littoral from 1978; Natura 2000 since 2006

walks:Sentier du Fenouillet (Domaine Fon.name: Sentier du Fenouillet (Domaine Foncin)
walks:Sentier du Fenouillet (Domaine Fon.hook: A roughly 4.5 km land-and-sea loop over the Fenouillet headland just behind Cavalaire, threading cork oaks and arbousiers (strawberry trees), dropping to wild coves and opening onto long views of the Îles d'Or. Some scrambly, narrow sea-edge sections — proper shoes.
walks:Sentier du Fenouillet (Domaine Fon.text: A roughly 4.5 km land-and-sea loop over the Fenouillet headland just behind Cavalaire, threading cork oaks and arbousiers (strawberry trees), dropping to wild coves and opening onto long views of the Îles d'Or. Some scrambly, narrow sea-edge sections — proper shoes. The headland is the Domaine Foncin, given to the nation early: Mireille Foncin — daughter of geographer and Alliance Française co-founder Pierre Foncin — bequeathed the land to the Conservatoire du littoral in 1977, one of the very first gifts it ever received, keeping this run of the Corniche des Maures from being villa'd over. It teaches one real thing — the arbousier flowers and ripens its fruit at the same time in autumn, which is why the maquis smells of honey then. Nearby Cap Nègre carries its own memory: French Commandos d'Afrique came ashore here on the night of 14–15 August 1944 as the US 3rd Infantry Division landed on the Cavalaire beaches during the Provence landings. Signal Land bequeathed to the Conservatoire du littoral by Mireille Foncin in 1977 (one of its first-ever donations)

walks:Pointe / high point of Cap Lardier.name: Pointe / high point of Cap Lardier
walks:Pointe / high point of Cap Lardier.hook: The panoramic crest of the cape reached mid-walk, giving a roughly 180° sweep over the Cap Camarat lighthouse, Cap Taillat, the Îles d'Hyères and du Levant, and back across the whole bay of Cavalaire.
walks:Pointe / high point of Cap Lardier.text: The panoramic crest of the cape reached mid-walk, giving a roughly 180° sweep over the Cap Camarat lighthouse, Cap Taillat, the Îles d'Hyères and du Levant, and back across the whole bay of Cavalaire. This is the payoff of the Trois-Caps hike and the clearest possible read of why the Conservatoire du littoral fought so hard for this land: from the top you see one green, empty cape holding out against a coast built up on every side. It is the longest protected coastal fringe of the three caps — about 6 km — laid out in front of you in a single glance. Honest note: on high fire-risk 'red' days in summer the Maures massif and these cape trails can be closed to walkers, so check the local prefectural access map before you set out. Signal 180° panorama over Cap Camarat, Cap Taillat and the Îles d'Hyères; the caps' longest protected fringe (~6 km)

calas:Cap Taillat.name: Cap Taillat
calas:Cap Taillat.hook: A former island tethered to the mainland by a thread-thin sand tombolo, with a turquoise swim beach on each side — the wild Baie de Briande to the west, and the l'Escalet-facing beach on the Ramatuelle side to the east. About 142 hectares of protected headland, no road, only the coast path.
calas:Cap Taillat.text: A former island tethered to the mainland by a thread-thin sand tombolo, with a turquoise swim beach on each side — the wild Baie de Briande to the west, and the l'Escalet-facing beach on the Ramatuelle side to the east. About 142 hectares of protected headland, no road, only the coast path. A Cavalaire gem · Ritual The Saint-Pierre fishermen's fête and the burning boat At the end of June the fishing community keeps the feast of their patron, Saint-Pierre: a procession through the streets, then a second procession out to sea from the Esplanade Sainte-Estelle, gathering fishermen, the old wooden pointus, divers and the SNSM lifeboats. A great sardinade is grilled on the beach at dusk, there is dancing, and the night ends — the oldest, strangest, most beautiful part — with an old boat set alight on the sand and left to burn against the dark water, a gesture that once meant solidarity with the poorest fisherman. Where — Cavalaire beach and port; late June (the Saint-Jean/Saint-Pierre weekend), run by the town's traditions association — exact dates vary yearly The isthmus is a living thing: east and west winds and the currents constantly redistribute its sand, and winter storms chew at it, so it is fenced with ganivelles to hold the dune together. The Conservatoire du littoral bought Cap Taillat in 1987 to head off a Club Med development, and it lies in the Port-Cros National Park adhesion zone. On 24 July 2017 a fire ran from Gigaro to l'Escalet, burning more than 500 hectares and reducing Cap Taillat to ash; the trail reopened only eight months later, after some 2,000 charred trees were felled and the path was rerouted to stop walkers trampling the recovering ground. The maquis greened back fast — but the umbrella pines will need decades to return. Signal Conservatoire du littoral property since 1987 (bought to block a Club Med); ~142.5 ha; devastated by the 24 July 2017 fire, trail reopened 2018

calas:Plage de la Briande.name: Plage de la Briande
calas:Plage de la Briande.hook: The last and wildest beach of La Croix-Valmer, on the Briande side of the Cap Taillat tombolo — a long curve of sand backed by dense maquis and parasol pines, with clear turquoise water and almost nothing built behind it.
calas:Plage de la Briande.text: The last and wildest beach of La Croix-Valmer, on the Briande side of the Cap Taillat tombolo — a long curve of sand backed by dense maquis and parasol pines, with clear turquoise water and almost nothing built behind it. Its famous 'alone in the world' feeling is a direct product of protection: no road reaches it, so the only way in is the sentier du littoral from the southernmost l'Escalet car park, about 45 minutes on foot. Because it sits inside the Conservatoire-protected Cap Lardier–Cap Taillat corridor, it will never be built on or serviced. Honest note: naturists frequent the wild coves you pass along the walk, but Briande itself is not an official naturist beach — read the signage. Signal Accessible only on foot via the sentier du littoral; inside the protected Lardier–Taillat corridor

calas:Plage & Sentier Sous-Marin de Bonp.name: Plage & Sentier Sous-Marin de Bonporteau
calas:Plage & Sentier Sous-Marin de Bonp.hook: Cavalaire's own wild cove — fine sand ringed by rock, eucalyptus, tamarisk and wild palms, with picnic tables in the pine shade. Just offshore runs a free underwater snorkel trail marked by buoys and submerged information panels, in the town's Marine Protected Area.
calas:Plage & Sentier Sous-Marin de Bonp.text: Cavalaire's own wild cove — fine sand ringed by rock, eucalyptus, tamarisk and wild palms, with picnic tables in the pine shade. Just offshore runs a free underwater snorkel trail marked by buoys and submerged information panels, in the town's Marine Protected Area. The cove lies inside the marine adhesion zone of the Port-Cros National Park, and the sentier sous-marin is open to any independent swimmer with a mask and snorkel — no ticket, no guide — following seven buoys over Posidonia seagrass, the meadow that is the nursery of the whole coast and the reason the water is so clear. Swimming here is unsupervised, which is exactly why it stays quiet while the town beaches fill (guided 'Esprit parc national' visits run Tuesday mornings in season). Signal Free marked underwater trail (7 buoys) in Cavalaire's Port-Cros National Park marine protected area (open in season)

calas:Plage du Figuier (the wild coves o.hook: A small, wild, white-sand cove tucked under the Corniche — one of a string of coves between the Rayol and Canadel beaches, loved by snorkelers for clear water over rock and Posidonia. Access is deliberately rough: steep, sometimes unmarked paths, described locally as 'sportif'.
calas:Plage du Figuier (the wild coves o.text: A small, wild, white-sand cove tucked under the Corniche — one of a string of coves between the Rayol and Canadel beaches, loved by snorkelers for clear water over rock and Posidonia. Access is deliberately rough: steep, sometimes unmarked paths, described locally as 'sportif'. These coves stay wild precisely because the slope is too steep and the trails are left rugged — the friction is the protection. Figuier sits just along from the Domaine du Rayol's Baie du Figuier, where the estate runs its guided sentier marin (the 'Jardin Marin', its marine landscape). It teaches one thing about this shore: the same Posidonia meadow that keeps the water so clear is what throws up the 'banquettes' of dead leaves on the sand each winter — a sign of a healthy sea, not a dirty one. Signal Wild snorkelling cove adjoining the Domaine du Rayol's Baie du Figuier marine trail; steep unmarked access

secret-gems:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
secret-gems:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin.hook: A ~20-hectare coastal estate whose 7 hectares of gardens, designed by landscape gardener Gilles Clément, recreate the landscapes of the world's Mediterranean-climate regions and their dry-climate kin — Chile, California, South Africa, south-west Australia, the Canaries and more — tumbling down the maquis slope to the sea, past a 1910 pergola and the Hôtel de la Mer.
secret-gems:Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin.text: A ~20-hectare coastal estate whose 7 hectares of gardens, designed by landscape gardener Gilles Clément, recreate the landscapes of the world's Mediterranean-climate regions and their dry-climate kin — Chile, California, South Africa, south-west Australia, the Canaries and more — tumbling down the maquis slope to the sea, past a 1910 pergola and the Hôtel de la Mer. The story is the terroir. In 1908 Alfred Courmes, a Bormes man who made his fortune in the colonies, bought about 40 hectares of wild maquis and had architect Guillaume Tronchet build the villas, the ancient-style pergola (1910) and the Hôtel de la Mer (1912–19); aviation magnate Henry Potez took it over in 1940. When it was about to be carved up for a 284-flat seaside development at the turn of the 1980s, residents formed 'Les Amis du Rayol-Canadel' (1980) and fought — and the Conservatoire du littoral bought the 20-hectare estate in 1989. Clément's radical idea was to stop fighting the drought and instead garden with plants from every Mediterranean climate on Earth. In summer the estate also runs the sentier marin, a guided mask-and-fins swim in the Baie du Figuier billed as the garden's marine landscape. Signal Founded 1908 by Alfred Courmes; saved by 'Les Amis du Rayol-Canadel' (est. 1980) and acquired by the Conservatoire du littoral in 1989; garden by Gilles Clément

secret-gems:Pardigon.name: Pardigon
secret-gems:Pardigon.hook: A green amphitheatre of former farmland and wetland set back behind the beach, backed by the Maures foothills and threaded by the Carrade stream — grazing, reeds and, buried under the grass, two excavated Roman villas.
secret-gems:Pardigon.text: A green amphitheatre of former farmland and wetland set back behind the beach, backed by the Maures foothills and threaded by the Carrade stream — grazing, reeds and, buried under the grass, two excavated Roman villas. It is the rarest thing on this coast: an undeveloped coastal plain in the middle of a summer-resort strip. It survived only after years of court fights — the Conseil d'État declared it a 'site remarquable du littoral', permanently non-buildable, which let the Conservatoire du littoral acquire it and make it inalienable in January 2011. Digs in the 1980s revealed two Roman wine estates straddling the Carrade, one on each commune. It's now being re-wilded: the dune cord rebuilt, the behind-dune wet meadows restored. Signal Made inalienable under the Conservatoire du littoral in January 2011 (declared a 'site remarquable du littoral'); Roman villas excavated in the 1980s

nightlife:La Rhumerie.name: La Rhumerie
nightlife:La Rhumerie.hook: A rum-and-cocktail bar on the marina quay — a bamboo-and-timber terrace over the moored boats, rum-based cocktails, apéro sharing boards, a small dance floor, and band or DJ nights that run late.
nightlife:La Rhumerie.text: A rum-and-cocktail bar on the marina quay — a bamboo-and-timber terrace over the moored boats, rum-based cocktails, apéro sharing boards, a small dance floor, and band or DJ nights that run late. Cavalaire is a marina town, and after dark its energy collects in the narrow gap between the moored boats and the quay — La Rhumerie is where that energy lands. It is the closest thing the town has to a club, and the honest tell is that it is a bar: apéro-boards, rum cocktails, a dance floor the size of a dinghy. What sets it apart here is the calendar — it works a long February-to-November season when most of the town shutters from autumn to Easter, so it is the port's near-constant. For an actual nightclub you leave: 30–40 minutes to Les Caves du Roy at the Byblos in St-Tropez, or the Ramatuelle/Pampelonne beach clubs (Nikki Beach and neighbours). Cavalaire itself does not pretend to that. Signal Nouveau Port, lot 151; open ~10 Feb–10 Nov, daily ~9:00–03:00; confirmed on Golfe de Saint-Tropez Tourisme and Petit Futé, Yelp listing updated Feb 2026

nightlife:Playa Mezcala.name: Playa Mezcala
nightlife:Playa Mezcala.hook: A feet-in-the-sand beach club near the Saint-Raphaël end of the bay — breakfast and lunch at the water's edge, a cocktail bar running through the day, tacos and pinsas, and, in high summer, dinner under the stars.
nightlife:Playa Mezcala.text: A feet-in-the-sand beach club near the Saint-Raphaël end of the bay — breakfast and lunch at the water's edge, a cocktail bar running through the day, tacos and pinsas, and, in high summer, dinner under the stars. Cavalaire exists as a resort because of one thing: a long, south-facing arc of sand, so the drink-with-a-view here happens on the beach, not on a rooftop — the town has none. Playa Mezcala grafts a Mexican-cantina conceit onto Var sand (the name, the mezcal, the tacos), exactly the borrowed-elsewhere styling you find all along this coast, even as the kitchen actually plays Mediterranean. Teach the register honestly: outside July and August the bar shuts around 19:00, so for most of the season this is apéro-and-sunset, not a late night; even in high summer it winds down at midnight over dinner, not at 2am. Come for the golden hour with your feet in the sand. Signal 822 avenue de Saint-Raphaël; beach club open daily ~8:30–19:00 (sunbeds and bar), dinner service to midnight only in July–August; official site playamezcala.com + Cavalaire tourism listing, active 2026

nightlife:Bar de La Ménado.name: Bar de La Ménado
nightlife:Bar de La Ménado.hook: The outdoor cocktail bar of the beachfront 4-star Hôtel La Ménado — a quiet terrace a stone's throw from the water, serving classic and house-signature cocktails alongside evening sharing platters.
nightlife:Bar de La Ménado.text: The outdoor cocktail bar of the beachfront 4-star Hôtel La Ménado — a quiet terrace a stone's throw from the water, serving classic and house-signature cocktails alongside evening sharing platters. This is the sunset-drink move, and its virtue is precisely what it is not: no DJ, no live band, no dance floor — just a terrace, a low sun on the water, and a barman's cocktail. In a town whose evening is modest by design, La Ménado is the calm end of the register, the anti-Rhumerie. The honest caveat is the calendar again: the bar opens only from 15 June to 15 September, so it is a high-summer address and nothing more — outside those three months this stretch of beachfront goes dark early. Signal 148 allée de la Plage; cocktail bar open 15 Jun–15 Sep per the hotel site (lamenado.com), 4-star hotel, beach 20 m away

nightlife:Les Escales Musicales.name: Les Escales Musicales
nightlife:Les Escales Musicales.hook: The town's real summer live-music engine — a free, roving concert series (jazz, soul, funk, pop) that turns the quays, Place des Bains and the squares into open-air stages through the season.
nightlife:Les Escales Musicales.text: The town's real summer live-music engine — a free, roving concert series (jazz, soul, funk, pop) that turns the quays, Place des Bains and the squares into open-air stages through the season. This is how a modest town does live music: not a fixed venue but a municipal series that moves, night to night, from the port to the squares — the actual answer to 'where's the live spot?' is 'wherever the Escale is this week.' It is the honest heart of Cavalaire's evening: free, outdoor, family-easy, and unmistakably seasonal, running only July into early September (it closes 1 Sept 2026 with PashGang on the Esplanade Sainte-Estelle). The bigger names — Hélène Ségara on 23 July, Julie Zenatti on 12 August — play the Sainte-Estelle esplanade the same summer, and those are free too; but the terroir-true thing is the roving programme on the quays. Signal Free itinerant concerts, Thu 2 Jul 2026 (The Color Gipsy, Place des Bains, 18:00) through 1 Sep (PashGang, Esplanade Sainte-Estelle); listed by the Ville de Cavalaire and Golfe de Saint-Tropez Tourisme

nightlife:Festival Face à la Mer.name: Festival Face à la Mer
nightlife:Festival Face à la Mer.hook: A small free jazz, blues and world-music festival staged over a few September evenings on the seafront esplanade — literally programmed, as the name says, facing the Mediterranean, with the silhouette of the Îles d'Hyères on the horizon.
nightlife:Festival Face à la Mer.text: A small free jazz, blues and world-music festival staged over a few September evenings on the seafront esplanade — literally programmed, as the name says, facing the Mediterranean, with the silhouette of the Îles d'Hyères on the horizon. The name is the whole idea: the stage looks straight out at the sea, so the horizon is the backdrop. What makes it worth timing a visit around is when it falls — early September, its fourth edition in 2026, once the August crush has drained away and Cavalaire is at its best and quietest. It is the shoulder-season send-off, and it teaches the real rhythm of this coast: the good nights here come after the crowds leave, not during them. Signal 4th edition, early September 2026, Esplanade Sainte-Estelle; free jazz/blues/world evenings; the 3rd edition ran 4–7 Sep 2025 (Ville de Cavalaire + Festivalenfrance listings)

nightlife:Marina Viva Plage.name: Marina Viva Plage
nightlife:Marina Viva Plage.hook: A private-beach restaurant and cocktail bar on the sand, with signature drinks timed to sunset — and one of the addresses that throws a party on the two nights the town genuinely does.
nightlife:Marina Viva Plage.text: A private-beach restaurant and cocktail bar on the sand, with signature drinks timed to sunset — and one of the addresses that throws a party on the two nights the town genuinely does. It earns its place for a specific, honest reason: on the two dates Cavalaire truly comes alive after dark — the Fête de la Musique on 21 June and Bastille Day on 14 July — the action is on the sand at the beach clubs, and Marina Viva is one that hosts it, staying open into the evening for the fireworks over the bay. That is the lesson about this town's nightlife in a sentence: it lives on the beach and on the calendar, not in a fixed club. Its bar otherwise winds down around 19:00, so any other night it is a sunset cocktail with your feet near the water — modest, seasonal, and none the worse for it. Signal Allée des Anthemis; private-beach restaurant + cocktail bar (creations by Thomas), season opens 24 Apr 2026; hosts a Fête de la Musique tapas-and-rosé evening (21 Jun) and a 14-Juillet fireworks evening per the venue site (marinavivaplage.fr)
